\paragraph{Limitations.}
Several limitations qualify these findings.
First, the function-level near-equivalence (1.24\pp{}) limits the practical advantage of \cls{} at that complexity scale---the reformulation matters most where generation failure modes activate, and function-level code largely avoids them.
Second, all experiments use a single model family (Qwen3); the scaling behavior may differ across architectures, and multi-model validation is needed.
Third, the oracle analysis assumes access to ground-truth test labels; in real deployment, the per-test advantage is upper-bounded by the actual classifier accuracy, which may be lower than the oracle rates.
Fourth, the P2P regression rate in SWE-bench Verified is too low ($\sim$1\% mean, 0\% median) for per-test P2P signals to be practically useful---the diagnostic advantage is currently limited to the F2P dimension.
Fifth, while error complementarity between \cls{} and \cwm{} is observed (oracle combination reaches 90.63\%), we have not yet exploited this in a working ensemble.

\paragraph{Future work.}
The error complementarity between \cls{} and \cwm{} (oracle 90.63\% vs.\ 87.51\% for \cls{} alone) motivates ensemble verification that routes to classification or generation based on predicted output complexity. The per-test failure signals produced by \cls{} enable a diagnostic re-repair pipeline: rather than discarding a failed patch, a repair agent could use per-test verdicts to localize the fault and generate targeted fixes. Repo-level evaluation, where \cwm{} failure modes are expected to be more acute, is in progress. Extending the analysis to multiple model families and integrating per-test scoring with test-time compute scaling systems (e.g., best-of-$N$ selection with per-test reranking) are natural next steps.
